description: Tension, compression, torsion, shear and bending — and how structures are reinforced against each.
content_html:
Forces in Structures and Products

Every physical product experiences forces during its use — the weight of books compresses a shelf, a twisted door handle experiences torsion, and a loaded bridge beam bends under traffic. Designers must understand the nature of these forces so they can choose the right material, shape and reinforcement strategy to ensure the product survives its intended service life without failing. Exam questions on this topic expect you to identify the type of stress acting on a component and justify a reinforcement choice with material and structural reasoning.

The Five Types of Stress

Tension is a pulling or stretching force. When two forces act along the same axis in opposite directions, pulling the material apart, the material is in tension. Examples: a rope suspending a load, a chain on a bicycle, the bottom flange of a loaded beam.

Compression is a pushing or squeezing force. When two forces act along the same axis pushing towards each other, the material is compressed and tends to shorten or buckle. Examples: the legs of a chair supporting a seated person, the columns of a building, the top flange of a loaded beam.

Torsion is a twisting force. When one end of a component is held fixed and a torque is applied to the other end, the material twists. A screwdriver shaft, a car drive shaft and a door handle spindle all experience torsion in normal use.

Shear is a cutting or sliding force where adjacent sections of a material tend to slide past each other. Scissors, chisels and bolts connecting structural members all experience shear. Shear is also the stress that causes a beam to fail by cracking vertically near its supports.

Bending occurs when a force acts perpendicular to the long axis of a component, causing it to curve. The top of a bent beam is in compression; the bottom is in tension. A shelf loaded at its centre, a diving board and a roof rafter all experience bending.

Key Fact

The five stresses are: tension (pulling apart), compression (pushing together), torsion (twisting), shear (sliding/cutting) and bending (top compressed, bottom stretched). A beam under a central load experiences both compression (top) and tension (bottom) simultaneously — this is a common exam question.

Reinforcement Methods by Material

Reinforcement increases a component’s resistance to failure without making it excessively heavy or expensive. Different material families use different structural techniques:

Papers and Boards

Corrugating paper creates a wavy internal layer that vastly increases bending stiffness. Corrugated cardboard packaging uses this principle: the fluted inner layer resists compression from the top surface, while the flat outer liners resist tension and provide a smooth printing surface. Without the corrugation, the same amount of paper would buckle under a fraction of the load.

Timbers

Laminating layers of wood (as in plywood or laminated veneer lumber) with the grain alternated at 90° distributes forces in multiple directions. A single piece of timber is strong along the grain but weak across it; plywood resists forces in both directions equally. Gussets — triangular corner reinforcements — are used at frame joints to resist racking (shear forces that push a rectangular frame into a parallelogram).

Metals

Metal sections can be formed into shapes that increase their second moment of area — effectively concentrating material away from the neutral axis to maximise resistance to bending. An I-beam (universal beam) is the classic example: the flanges are far from the centre, giving very high bending resistance with minimal material. Ribs on metal enclosures (such as those on the inside of cast aluminium gear housings) perform the same function, resisting bending while keeping the wall thin and light. Hollow box sections resist both bending and torsion more efficiently than solid sections of the same mass.

Polymers

Polymers are often reinforced at points of weakness using additional wall thickness, ribbing on the inside of moulded parts, or by embedding them in a matrix of fibres. Ribs on the inside of an injection-moulded plastic casing resist bending without increasing the outer wall thickness (which would cause sink marks and extend cooling time). Glass-reinforced polymer (GRP) uses glass fibres within a polyester resin matrix; the fibres resist tension that the resin alone could not withstand.

When a beam bends, stress is highest at the top (compression) and bottom (tension) surfaces and nearly zero at the neutral axis in the middle. An I-beam exploits this by placing the majority of its material at the flanges (top and bottom), where stress is highest, and using only a thin web in the middle where stress is low. The same mass of steel in a rectangular section would be far weaker in bending because much of the material sits near the neutral axis doing little structural work.

This principle also explains why hollow tubes resist bending and torsion better than solid rods of the same cross-sectional area: material near the centre contributes little to resisting these forces. Bicycle frames use aluminium or carbon fibre tubes for exactly this reason — light, stiff and strong because the material is distributed at the outer surface where stresses are highest.

Textiles and Fibres

Interfacing is a woven or non-woven fabric bonded to the reverse of a textile to add stiffness — used in shirt collars, waistbands and the structured panels of bags. Webbing — tightly woven strips of nylon, polyester or polypropylene — is used for straps and harnesses because it has very high tensile strength along its length. Quilting (sandwiching insulation between fabric layers, held by stitching) resists delamination and maintains the insulating layer’s thickness under repeated compression.

Key Fact

Reinforcement works by distributing stress over a larger area or redirecting it into a form the material can withstand. Corrugating (paper/boards), laminating (timber), ribbing and I-section profiles (metals), ribbing inside moulded parts (polymers) and interfacing/webbing (textiles) are all exam-required reinforcement techniques. Know at least one technique per material family.

The most common error in exam answers on this topic is confusing bending with compression. A shelf that sags in the middle is bending, not simply compressing — the top surface is in compression and the bottom is in tension. Stating only “the shelf is compressed by the books” misses the structure of the stress and will only score partial marks.

A second common error is describing reinforcement too vaguely. “Make it thicker” is not a reinforcement technique — it simply adds material without changing the distribution of stress. A specific answer names the structural form: “adding ribs to the inside of the moulded casing increases bending stiffness without increasing wall thickness, avoiding sink marks in the surface finish.” This level of specificity is required for the top mark band on applied questions.
exam_tip_html: For questions asking you to identify the type of stress acting on a component, look at the direction and effect of the force: pulling apart = tension; pushing together = compression; twisting = torsion; sliding = shear; curving the component = bending. For questions asking you to ‘justify’ a reinforcement method, name the technique (corrugating, ribbing, laminating, etc.), state which stress it resists and explain the structural reason — not just “it makes it stronger.” A 6-mark explain answer that names a material-specific technique and explains the mechanism of reinforcement will reach the Secure band or above.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The five stresses are tension (pull), compression (push), torsion (twist), shear (slide/cut) and bending (top compressed, bottom stretched). A beam under a central load experiences both compression and tension simultaneously.
  • Reinforcement techniques are material-specific: corrugating (paper/boards), laminating (timber), ribs and I-sections (metals/polymers), interfacing and webbing (textiles).
  • Effective reinforcement redistributes stress over a larger area or concentrates material where stress is highest — not just adding thickness throughout.

practice_questions.text:
A bicycle chain is pulled tight between the pedal gear and the rear wheel gear while the cyclist pedals. What type of stress is the chain experiencing?
A) Compression
B) Torsion
C) Tension
D) Shear
State the type of stress acting on the top surface of a wooden shelf that sags under the weight of heavy books.
practice_questions.marks: Compression. [1 mark] (The top of a bent beam/shelf is in compression; the bottom is in tension. Accept 'bending' as the overall stress type with 'compression at the top surface' for full credit.)

practice_questions.text: Describe how corrugating a sheet of card increases its resistance to bending.
practice_questions.marks:
• The corrugated layer creates a wavy internal structure with peaks and troughs. [1 mark]
• The vertical elements of the corrugation resist compressive forces acting from above. [1 mark]
• This increases the card's stiffness under bending loads without significantly increasing the material mass. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain why an I-beam profile resists bending forces more efficiently than a solid rectangular section of the same mass of steel.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• When a beam bends, stress is highest at the top (compression) and bottom (tension) surfaces and nearly zero at the neutral axis in the centre. [1 mark]
• An I-beam concentrates its material in the flanges at the top and bottom, where bending stress is highest. [1 mark]
• The thin web in the middle carries little of the bending load, so placing material there (as a solid section does) is structurally inefficient. [1 mark]
• The same mass of steel in an I-section therefore provides far greater bending resistance than a solid rectangular section. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A designer is creating a rigid shoulder bag from a woven cotton fabric. Explain, with reference to specific reinforcement techniques, how the structural integrity of the bag can be improved so that it withstands tension in the strap and prevents the base from deforming under load.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Nylon or polypropylene webbing should be used for the shoulder strap because webbing has very high tensile strength along its length and will resist the tension created by the weight of the bag's contents. [2 marks]
• Interfacing bonded to the base panel adds rigidity, distributing the compressive and bending forces from the loaded bag contents over a wider area rather than allowing the fabric to deform. [2 marks]
• Reinforced stitching at stress concentration points — where the strap attaches to the bag body — distributes shear forces that would otherwise cause the strap to tear out. [1 mark]
• An internal base board or rigid panel can be inserted to resist the shear and bending loads at the base. [1 mark]
[6 marks — Mastering: Three techniques named with material-specific justification linked to the specific stress type each resists. Secure: Two techniques with justification. Developing: One technique named with basic explanation. Emerging: Vague suggestion ('make it stronger') without technique or stress type.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using glass-reinforced polymer (GRP) compared to sheet aluminium for the bodywork panels of a sports car.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of GRP over sheet aluminium:
• GRP can be formed into complex double-curvature shapes (such as curved body panels) without the expensive tooling and pressing equipment required to shape aluminium.
• GRP has a lower density than aluminium (approximately 1.8 g/cm³ vs 2.7 g/cm³), reducing the vehicle's overall mass and improving performance.
• GRP does not corrode, reducing maintenance requirements and extending panel life in wet climates.
• GRP panels can be repaired with filler and resin without specialist equipment; dented aluminium panels often require panel beating and repainting.
Disadvantages of GRP:
• GRP has lower stiffness than aluminium for the same thickness; panels may flex or vibrate at high speed unless additional thickness or ribbing is added.
• GRP is more difficult to recycle at end of life; thermoset resins cannot be remelted, whereas aluminium is highly recyclable.
• GRP is more flammable than aluminium and may release toxic fumes if the vehicle catches fire.
• Surface finish on GRP requires gel-coat application and careful mould preparation; aluminium can be anodised or painted directly.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained balanced discussion with at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages specific to sports car bodywork. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development, limited balance. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial response.]

flashcard_questions.q: What type of stress is a rope under when it suspends a heavy weight?
What type of stress acts on the legs of a chair when someone sits on it?
What type of stress does a door handle spindle experience when the handle is turned?
What type of stress do scissors blades exert on paper as they cut?
When a beam bends under a central load, the top surface is in _____ and the bottom surface is in _____.
How does corrugating increase the stiffness of cardboard?
flashcard_questions.a: The wavy internal layer resists compressive bending forces without significantly adding mass.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is plywood stronger than a single piece of timber of the same thickness?
flashcard_questions.a: Alternating grain directions resist forces from multiple directions, not just along the grain.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is an I-beam more efficient in bending than a solid rectangular section of the same mass?
flashcard_questions.a: Material is concentrated at the flanges where bending stress is highest; the low-stress centre is minimised.

flashcard_questions.q: What is interfacing used for in textile products?
flashcard_questions.a: To add stiffness to fabric layers, resisting deformation in panels such as shirt collars.

flashcard_questions.q: What material is webbing typically made from, and what stress does it primarily resist?
flashcard_questions.a: Nylon or polypropylene; tension along its length.

glossary_terms.definition: A pulling force acting along the length of a material, stretching it.
A squeezing or pushing force that acts to shorten a material along its length.
A twisting force applied around the long axis of a material.
A force that causes one part of a material to slide relative to an adjacent part, like scissors cutting through paper.
A force that creates a combination of tension and compression across the cross-section of a material, causing it to curve.
A manufacturing technique that forms a material into a series of parallel folds or waves, significantly increasing stiffness without adding weight.
The bonding of thin layers of material together with grain directions alternated, increasing strength and reducing the tendency to warp.
Structural ridges or walls added to a surface to resist bending without adding solid thickness.
A stiff material bonded to a fabric layer to increase its structural rigidity and resistance to deformation.
